title: The Angel ended ... So Charming left his voice (lines added in 1674)
short: These opening lines were added in the second edition of 1674, when Milton divided the original ten books into twelve.
body: The first edition of 1667 had ten books; Raphael's account of the creation and Adam's reply formed a single Book VII. For the second edition of 1674 Milton split that book (and the original Book X) to make twelve books, as Virgil's Aeneid has, and added these four lines to bridge the break: 'The Angel ended, and in Adams Eare So Charming left his voice, that he a while Thought him still speaking, still stood fixt to hear'. The Dartmouth edition notes the addition; the square brackets in this text mark it. Verity remarks that 'stood' probably means 'remained' rather than describing Adam's posture. The image of the listener spellbound after the voice has stopped also suggests the effect Milton hoped his own poem would have.

anchor: Her Husband the Relater she preferr'd
title: Eve leaves: 'Her Husband the Relater she preferr'd'
short: Eve withdraws from the astronomical discussion, not because she cannot understand it, but because she prefers to hear it from Adam, with 'conjugal Caresses'.
body: When Adam turns to astronomy, Eve rises to tend her flowers. The narrator is careful to explain: she went not 'as not with such discourse Delighted, or not capable her eare Of what was high', but because she preferred to hear it later from Adam, who 'would intermix Grateful digressions, and solve high dispute With conjugal Caresses'. The passage has been read in opposite ways: as condescending, since it sends the woman out when science begins, or as a defence of Eve's intelligence and an endorsement of learning through love and conversation, which Milton in his divorce tracts called the chief end of marriage. Her absence also means she does not hear Raphael's warnings at first hand, which matters in Book IX, where she must rely on what Adam has told her.

anchor: Cycle and Epicycle, Orb in Orb
title: Centric and Eccentric ... Cycle and Epicycle, Orb in Orb
short: Raphael mocks the elaborate devices of Ptolemaic astronomy, circles on circles invented 'to save appearances', which God may laugh at.
body: Raphael tells Adam that God has left the fabric of the heavens to men's disputes, perhaps 'to move His laughter at thir quaint Opinions wide' (Psalm 2:4), when they 'come to model Heav'n And calculate the Starrs' and, 'to save appeerances', gird the sphere 'With Centric and Eccentric scribl'd o're, Cycle and Epicycle, Orb in Orb'. Verity explains that these were devices of the Ptolemaic system for preserving circular motion: eccentric spheres have centres other than the earth, and an epicycle is a small circle whose centre moves round a larger one (the deferent). 'To save appearances' translates the astronomers' phrase 'to save the phenomena'; the Dartmouth edition quotes Donne's complaint that such devices tear the firmament into pieces. Verity notes the contemptuous 'scribl'd'.

title: What if the Sun Be Centre to the World ... three different Motions
short: Raphael raises the Copernican hypothesis, that the sun is the centre and the earth a planet with three motions, without affirming it.
body: Having mocked the Ptolemaic devices, Raphael offers the alternative as a question: 'What if the Sun Be Centre to the World, and other Starrs By his attractive vertue and thir own Incited, dance about him various rounds?' The 'Planet Earth' may move 'Insensibly three different Motions'. Verity, quoting Newton, explains the three Copernican motions: daily rotation, the annual orbit round the sun, and a third motion keeping the axis parallel. He adds that Milton's poem generally assumes the Ptolemaic universe but leans towards Copernicus here. The Dartmouth edition stresses that Raphael introduces the view 'strictly as a speculation': 'Not that I so affirm' (8.117). The point is less to settle astronomy than to show that it does not matter for Adam's happiness: 'whether Heav'n move or Earth, Imports not' (8.70-71).

title: other Suns ... Dream not of other Worlds
short: Raphael raises the possibility of inhabited moons and other suns with their planets, then tells Adam not to dream of them.
body: Raphael speculates that the moon may be inhabited, with 'Fields and Inhabitants', and that 'other Suns perhaps With thir attendant Moons thou wilt descrie' (8.144-49). Verity notes the contemporary debate: Keightley thought Milton meant Jupiter and Saturn, whose moons Galileo had discovered, but Verity prefers the theory reported by Burton that the fixed stars are suns with their own planets, a view Kepler rejected. The plurality of worlds was a live and controversial idea in the 1600s, as the Dartmouth edition notes. Yet Raphael ends by redirecting Adam: 'Sollicit not thy thoughts with matters hid', 'Dream not of other Worlds, what Creatures there Live, in what state, condition or degree, Contented that thus farr hath been reveal'd Not of Earth onely but of highest Heav'n'.

title: Heav'n is for thee too high To know what passes there; be lowlie wise
short: Raphael's counsel of intellectual humility: think of what concerns you and your being, not of what God has hidden.
body: 'Heav'n is for thee too high To know what passes there; be lowlie wise: Think onely what concerns thee and thy being'. The phrase was echoed by Wordsworth ('made lowly wise', Ode to Duty), as Verity notes, and the Dartmouth edition cites Du Bartas, 'Be sober wise'. Adam accepts the lesson gracefully: the 'prime Wisdom' is 'to know That which before us lies in daily life' (8.192-94). The passage has been read as anti-scientific obscurantism, but it is more precisely a lesson about the ordering of knowledge, consistent with 'Knowledge is as food' (7.126): curiosity is good when it serves praise and duty, dangerous when it becomes a desire for godlike knowledge. Satan's temptation of Eve (9.679-732) will attack exactly this boundary.

anchor: how came I thus, how here?
title: Adam's first awakening: 'how came I thus, how here?'
short: Adam recalls his creation: he looked up to the sky, sprang upright, and at once inferred a Maker, unlike Satan, who denied one.
body: Adam tells Raphael how he woke 'As new wak't from soundest sleep', turned his eyes 'Strait toward Heav'n', and sprang upright 'By quick instinctive motion'. He asks the sun, earth and creatures to tell him who made him: 'Tell, if ye saw, how came I thus, how here? Not of my self; by some great Maker then'. Verity cross-refers to Satan's claim to be 'self-begot' (5.857-58) and glosses 'from whom I have that thus I move and live' from Acts 17:28, 'in him we live, and move, and have our being'. The Dartmouth edition invites comparison with Eve's first moments (4.449-91): Adam looks up to heaven, Eve looks down into a pool. The contrast has been read as a hierarchy, and also as two equally natural first experiences of selfhood.

anchor: I nam'd them, as they pass'd
title: I nam'd them, as they pass'd, and understood Thir Nature
short: Adam names the animals (Genesis 2:19-20) with instant understanding of their natures, a sign of the perfect wisdom of unfallen man.
body: God brings the beasts to Adam 'to receave From thee thir Names', and Adam names them 'as they pass'd, and understood Thir Nature, with such knowledg God endu'd My sudden apprehension'. Verity quotes Milton's Christian Doctrine (1.7): only extraordinary wisdom could have named the whole animal creation with such sudden intelligence; and Tetrachordon, where Adam's wisdom to know creatures by their properties implies he could also recognise the fit partner provided for him. The naming follows Genesis 2:19-20, where the next words are 'but for Adam there was not found an help meet for him', which the Dartmouth edition notes. Language before the Fall is imagined as perfectly adequate to things; after Babel, Michael says, it will be confused (12.52-62).

title: In solitude What happiness ... Collateral love, and deerest amitie
short: Adam asks God for a companion: God is perfect 'through all numbers absolute, though One', but man is incomplete alone and needs an equal for 'rational delight'.
body: Adam boldly argues with God: 'In solitude What happiness, who can enjoy alone?' Among unequals there can be no 'societie', 'Harmonie or true delight', only fellowship 'fit to participate All rational delight'. God, he reasons, is 'through all numbers absolute, though One', a Latinism Verity explains from 'omnibus numeris absolutus', perfect in every part, but man is defective in unity and needs 'Collateral love, and deerest amitie'. Verity reads lines 405-07 as further evidence of Milton's Arianism. The Dartmouth edition shows how closely Adam's language matches Milton's divorce tracts, where the chief end of marriage is 'an apt and cheerful conversation' and Genesis 2:18, 'It is not good that the man should be alone', is interpreted at length. God replies that he was testing Adam, and approves his request.

title: From thence a Rib, with cordial spirits warme
short: Adam, in a trance, sees God take a rib from his left side, near the heart, and fashion Eve from it.
body: God closes Adam's eyes but leaves open 'the Cell Of Fancie my internal sight', so that Adam sees, as in a trance (Verity compares the 'deep sleep' of Genesis 2:21, which Newton explained as a trance), the Creator open 'my left side' and take 'a Rib, with cordial spirits warme, And Life-blood streaming fresh'. Verity quotes Newton: Scripture says only 'one of his ribs', but Milton follows interpreters who chose the left side as nearer the heart (Latin cor, hence 'cordial'). In Tetrachordon Milton noted that no other wife was ever moulded from her husband's rib, so Adam and Eve were closer than any later couple. The Dartmouth edition notes the weaving of the Genesis 1 and 2 accounts, and Satan's wound on the left side at Sin's birth (2.755) is a dark parody.

title: Bone of my Bone, Flesh of my Flesh, my Self Before me
short: Adam greets Eve with the words of Genesis 2:23, adding 'my Self Before me', a phrase that will return at the Fall.
body: When Eve is brought to him Adam cries: 'I now see Bone of my Bone, Flesh of my Flesh, my Self Before me; Woman is her Name, of Man Extracted; for this cause he shall forgoe Father and Mother, and to his Wife adhere; And they shall be one Flesh, one Heart, one Soule'. Verity notes the sources in Genesis 2:23-24, Matthew 19:4-6 and Mark 10:6-8, and that 'adhere' follows the Vulgate 'adhaerebit' for 'cleave'. The Dartmouth edition observes that none of the biblical texts says 'my Self'. That addition is decisive later: in Book IX Adam chooses to fall with Eve because 'Flesh of Flesh, Bone of my Bone thou art' and 'to lose thee were to lose my self' (9.914-15, 959).

title: the amorous Bird of Night Sung Spousal, and bid haste the Eevning Starr
short: The nightingale sings the wedding song and hastens the evening star, Venus, whose rising was the classical signal to light the bridal torch.
body: Adam describes his wedding night: the earth and heavens give signs of joy, and 'the amorous Bird of Night Sung Spousal, and bid haste the Eevning Starr On his Hill top, to light the bridal Lamp'. The evening star (Hesperus, the planet Venus) was the traditional signal for the wedding procession in classical marriage songs; Verity cites Catullus' epithalamium (poem 62, 'Vesper adest') and the Dartmouth edition, quoting Hughes, adds Spenser's Epithalamion. Verity notes that the omens of heaven and earth are modelled on classical poets, and that the same signs reverse at the Fall, when 'Sky lowr'd' and nature groans (9.782-84, 1000-04). The nightingale ('amorous Bird of Night') is, Verity notes, Milton's favourite bird.

title: transported I behold, Transported touch ... Too much of Ornament
short: Adam confesses that Eve's beauty overwhelms his reason: she seems 'absolute', wisest and best, and he wonders whether Nature gave her 'Too much of Ornament'.
body: Adam admits to Raphael that, though 'superior and unmov'd' by other pleasures, 'here Farr otherwise, transported I behold, Transported touch'. He knows Eve is inferior 'in the mind And inward Faculties', yet in her presence she seems 'so absolute' that 'what she wills to do or say, Seems wisest, vertuousest, discreetest, best', and wonders if Nature, in making her, bestowed 'Too much of Ornament'. Verity compares the chorus of Samson Agonistes (1025-30) on woman's 'outward ornament' and states that this is Milton's own view of the sexes, while noting Tennyson's contrary 'diverse'. The Dartmouth edition suggests that Milton traces the hyperbole of Petrarchan love poetry to Adam's error. The confession is the clearest warning in the poem of the weakness that will make Adam fall.

title: To whom the Angel with contracted brow. Accuse not Nature
short: Raphael frowns and corrects Adam: Nature has done her part; Adam must not let an 'outside' subject him, but rely on self-esteem grounded in reason.
body: Raphael answers 'with contracted brow', a frown (Verity cites Cicero's 'contrahere frontem'): 'Accuse not Nature, she hath don her part; Do thou but thine'. Eve is 'An outside? fair no doubt, and worthy well Thy cherishing, thy honouring, and thy love, Not thy subjection'; Adam should rely on 'self-esteem, grounded on just and right Well manag'd'. Verity cites Ephesians 5:28-29 for cherishing and 1 Corinthians 11:3 ('the head of the woman is the man') and notes that the passage anticipates the Son's judgment after the Fall, 'Was shee thy God, that her thou didst obey?' (10.145-56). The Dartmouth edition contrasts Hermes' warning to Odysseus and Mercury's to Aeneas, who are told to leave their women: Raphael tells Adam to stay with Eve but not be subdued.

title: Love ... hath his seat In Reason ... is the scale By which to heav'nly Love thou maist ascend
short: True love is rational and a ladder to heavenly love, the Platonic doctrine of Symposium in Christian form; carnal passion alone is shared with beasts.
body: Raphael distinguishes the 'sense of touch whereby mankind Is propagated', common to 'Cattel and each Beast', from true love, which 'refines The thoughts, and heart enlarges, hath his seat In Reason, and is judicious, is the scale By which to heav'nly Love thou maist ascend'. Verity traces the idea to Plato's Symposium, with its two kinds of love, heavenly and common, and its ladder of ascent, transmitted through Spenser's Hymne of Heavenly Love and Italian Neoplatonism; he also cites Dante's distinction of natural and rational love (Purgatorio 17-18). 'Scale' means ladder (Latin scala), the same image as the scale of nature in 5.483-509. Adam replies, a little defensively, that it is not her beauty but her 'graceful acts' and 'Union of Mind' that delight him.

title: Celestial rosie red, Loves proper hue ... Union of Pure with Pure
short: Asked whether angels love, Raphael blushes and answers that they do, more completely than humans: spirits mingle wholly, with no obstacle of flesh.
body: Adam asks whether 'Heav'nly Spirits' love and how. Raphael answers 'with a smile that glow'd Celestial rosie red, Loves proper hue': whatever pure pleasure the body gives humans, angels enjoy 'In eminence, and obstacle find none Of membrane, joynt, or limb', for 'Easier then Air with Air, if Spirits embrace, Total they mix, Union of Pure with Pure Desiring'. The passage expresses Milton's monism: spirit is a refined form of matter, so angelic love is a fuller version of human love, not its opposite. Verity compares Wordsworth's 'such love as spirits feel'; the Dartmouth edition glosses 'virtual' and compares Lucretius on the frustrations of bodily union (De Rerum Natura 4). Whether Raphael's blush is embarrassment or the natural colour of love has been much discussed.
